title: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution with data in hollow-core fiber
authors: Yue Luo, Sheng Liu, Yun-Ru Fan, Da-Wei Ge, Zhi-Yang Liu, Hao Li, Si Shen, Zi-Chang Zhang, Hai-Zhi Song, Li-Xing You, Tao Zhou, Kai Guo, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: The coexistence of quantum information and classical signals in a single fiber is essential for future quantum networks that leverage the well-established optical fiber infrastructure. Although multiplexing technologies can separate quantum and classical signals, pure silica core fibers (PSCFs) remain fundamentally limited by the high nonlinearity, which generates substantial Raman scattering and four-wave mixing noise. Hollow-core fibers (HCFs), guiding light predominantly in air, offer an attractive solution with intrinsically ultra-low nonlinearity and strongly suppressed nonlinear noise. In this work, we demonstrate the entanglement-based key coexisting with data over an 18-km HCF link. We achieve time-encoded high-dimensional quantum key distribution (HD-QKD) carrying 0 dBm of bidirectional received power, corresponding to a theoretical data capacity of up to 2.3 Tbps. During 24 hours of continuous operation, an average secret key rate (SKR) of 10.56 kbps is obtained. Theoretical analysis further predicts SKRs above 135 kbps over transmission distances exceeding 200 km using state-of-the-art low-loss HCFs. These results show significantly improved performance compared with PSCF-based systems and highlight the potential of HCFs for scalable quantum-classical coexistence compatible with the architectures of established fiber-optic networks.
summary: The paper demonstrates that Hollow-Core Fibers (HCFs) are superior to traditional silica fibers for coexisting quantum key distribution and classical data transmission due to their ultra-low nonlinearity. Through experiments over 18 km, they achieved a stable secret key rate while maintaining high theoretical capacity estimates. This work validates HCFs as a scalable platform for future quantum internet infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge is enabling quantum key distribution (QKD) and classical data transmission to coexist reliably within a single optical fiber for future quantum networks.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated entanglement-based HD-QKD coexisting with data over an 18-km Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF) link, achieving an average Secret Key Rate of 10.56 kbps and predicting rates above 135 kbps over 200 km using state-of-the-art HCFs.
method: The authors employed time-encoded High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution (HD-QKD) protocols, characterizing noise sources like Raman scattering by comparing performance in HCF versus conventional Single-Mode Fiber (SMF).
model_or_system: The physical platform is the Hollow-Core Fiber (HCF), which guides light predominantly in air, offering intrinsically ultra-low nonlinearity compared to Pure Silica Core Fibers (PSCFs) that suffer from noise like Raman scattering and four-wave mixing.
key_observables: Secret Key Rate (SKR), Coincidence-to-Accidental Ratio (CAR), Quantum Bit Error Rates (QBERs), and theoretical data capacity (up to 2.3 Tbps).
important_parameters: 18-km link length, $0 	ext{ dBm}$ bidirectional received power, time-encoded dimension ($d=8$), and predicted SKR $> 135 	ext{ kbps}$ over $200+	ext{ km}$.
main_assumptions: The theoretical analysis relies on the availability of state-of-the-art low-loss HCFs to maintain high performance over long distances.
figures_summary: Figures compare SMF and HCF performance, illustrate the experimental setup for simultaneous quantum/classical transmission, and show noise power spectral density and coincidence counts vs. classical channel wavelength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the coexistence problem in standard fibers to proposing HCFs as a solution; it details experimental measurements of noise suppression and QKD performance over 18 km; finally, it provides theoretical scaling analysis predicting long-distance capabilities using low-loss models.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems because it addresses the critical engineering challenge of integrating fragile quantum signals with high-power classical channels in a practical fiber infrastructure, which requires detailed noise characterization.
